      <p class="ws-sub">A ranked backlog of policies to encode as versioned machine-readable context primitives, plus the human escape valves.</p>
    </div>

    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.html#sec-organizational-policy-gap">#sec-organizational-policy-gap</a>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>Organizational Policy: The Permanent Governance Gap</h2>
    <p>One limitation of AI-assisted governance that no model improvement will resolve: organizational policy awareness lives nowhere in training data. An agent can enforce coding standards from a rules file. It can run 22 automated policy checks in CI. But it cannot know that your organization's legal team requires review for any feature touching PII, or that a PR linking a personal asset from a corporate repository creates a compliance risk — unless that policy is explicitly encoded in the context layer. This is why governance primitives must include organizational policies, not just technical standards. Part III makes the underlying mechanism concrete: Chapter 12 explains how to instrument the codebase so policy gates fail loudly rather than silently, Chapter 16 explains how those gates sit at the seam where the agent's action meets the deterministic system, and Chapter 21 explains how policy primitives are versioned and shared the way application code is. The Growth Engine case study documents this finding in detail: fifteen agent personas across seven expert panels missed a compliance constraint that a human caught in seconds.</p>
    <span class="prior-src">handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd L153-157</span>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-foot-quote">
    "fifteen personas across seven panels missed it because organizational policy is not in the training data." (ch05 L163)
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    On the wall, list one policy or constraint per row; use the printed seeds as prompts and add every relevant policy of your own. Record its operative rule, current location and encoding, owners, enforcement path, prevalence, stakes and encoding date. For every human escape valve, name the person and the route the workflow uses to reach them. Complete Block B separately with the facts agents must restate correctly, their verified source, owner and review date; a person must verify each fact before downstream use.
  </div>

    Source: <b>Governance for AI-Assisted Delivery</b>, <i>The Organizational Knowledge Gap</i> &middot;
    <code>handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd</code> L153-177 &middot;
    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.html#sec-organizational-policy-gap">#sec-organizational-policy-gap</a>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>Organizational Policy: The Permanent Governance Gap</h2>
    <p>One limitation of AI-assisted governance that no model improvement will resolve: organizational policy awareness lives nowhere in training data. An agent can enforce coding standards from a rules file. It can run 22 automated policy checks in CI. But it cannot know that your organization's legal team requires review for any feature touching PII, or that a PR linking a personal asset from a corporate repository creates a compliance risk — unless that policy is explicitly encoded in the context layer. This is why governance primitives must include organizational policies, not just technical standards. Part III makes the underlying mechanism concrete: Chapter 12 explains how to instrument the codebase so policy gates fail loudly rather than silently, Chapter 16 explains how those gates sit at the seam where the agent's action meets the deterministic system, and Chapter 21 explains how policy primitives are versioned and shared the way application code is. The Growth Engine case study documents this finding in detail: fifteen agent personas across seven expert panels missed a compliance constraint that a human caught in seconds.</p>
    <span class="prior-src">handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd L153-157</span>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-foot-quote">
    "fifteen personas across seven panels missed it because organizational policy is not in the training data." (ch05 L163)
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    Continue the policy backlog. Use these rows for the remaining seed policies and add any more your organisation names; the seeds are prompts, not the scope. Record each actual policy name and document identifier. Use another copy of this sheet for additional policies. Complete both owners independently and connect every human escape valve to a named person and reachable route.
  </div>

    <div>
      <h1>Organisational Policy Encoding Inventory: What Your Agents Cannot Know</h1>
      <p class="ws-sub">Block B — the load-bearing facts register. Short by design: facts agents will restate across deliverables.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="ws-meta">

  <div class="ws-source">
    Source: <b>Governance for AI-Assisted Delivery</b>, <i>The Organizational Knowledge Gap</i> &middot;
    <code>handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd</code> L153-177 &middot;
    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.html#sec-organizational-policy-gap">#sec-organizational-policy-gap</a>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>Organizational Policy: The Permanent Governance Gap</h2>
    <p>One limitation of AI-assisted governance that no model improvement will resolve: organizational policy awareness lives nowhere in training data. An agent can enforce coding standards from a rules file. It can run 22 automated policy checks in CI. But it cannot know that your organization's legal team requires review for any feature touching PII, or that a PR linking a personal asset from a corporate repository creates a compliance risk — unless that policy is explicitly encoded in the context layer. This is why governance primitives must include organizational policies, not just technical standards. Part III makes the underlying mechanism concrete: Chapter 12 explains how to instrument the codebase so policy gates fail loudly rather than silently, Chapter 16 explains how those gates sit at the seam where the agent's action meets the deterministic system, and Chapter 21 explains how policy primitives are versioned and shared the way application code is. The Growth Engine case study documents this finding in detail: fifteen agent personas across seven expert panels missed a compliance constraint that a human caught in seconds.</p>
    <span class="prior-src">handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd L153-157</span>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-foot-quote">
    "fifteen personas across seven panels missed it because organizational policy is not in the training data." (ch05 L163)
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    For each fact, write the value exactly as it must appear, cite its system of record (never another generated artefact), name its owner and review date, and have a person verify it before any downstream worksheet or agent primitive uses it. Tick and date column 20 only after human verification. Add other fact classes in the open rows.
  </div>
